design_detail: Cross-sectional self-report survey of 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US addiction treatment facilities, collected at routine admission by a third-party outcomes-tracking system (Trac9, NLW Partners, LLC) and analysed de-identified. The 1,163 who said they probably or definitely used fentanyl were asked the shortest time they had ever waited after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine (and, as a comparator, methadone), whether they had experienced withdrawal symptoms (none, mild, moderate, severe) when taking it after fentanyl, and whether it decreased their withdrawal. Severe withdrawal was compared across waiting-time categories by binary logistic regression; no covariates are reported and the reference category is not named (the editors reproduce every printed odds ratio exactly with the within-1-month group as reference). Survey dates, questionnaire wording and response rate are not reported. Read from the PMC author manuscript.
can_establish: How often people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl recalled severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine (or methadone) after fentanyl, and how that recall varied with the shortest wait after fentanyl that they reported.
cannot_establish: The incidence of precipitated withdrawal (withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine is not separated from withdrawal it failed to relieve, and the occasion, dose, formulation and supervision are unknown), that waiting longer prevents it (the shortest wait ever is not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal and nothing is adjusted), or how often it occurs with supervised standard or low-dose starts.

sample.recruitment: Clinic: people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at one of 49 US addiction treatment facilities; a third-party aggregation system (Trac9, NLW Partners, LLC) collected the data to track treatment outcomes as part of routine admissions (Methods, Sample and Assessments, PDF p. 2).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: The fentanyl questions were asked of people whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl before treatment (PDF p. 2). No other criteria, survey period, facility types or states are reported.
sample.demographics: Of the 1,163 who reported fentanyl use: mean age 30.77 years (SD 10.23), 70.6% male (821), 80.4% White (935); 43.9% (510) said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission (Results, Patient Demographics, PDF p. 3). The paragraph opens with the 1,679, but these percentages are of the 1,163 (editors' calculation); the whole cohort is not described.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). No response rate or item-completion figures are reported.
sample.selection_effects: People entering treatment at facilities using one outcomes system, which are not described; two authors are affiliated with Ashley Addiction Treatment. People who used fentanyl but did not enter these programmes are absent. Of the 1,163, 421 (36.2%) had never taken buprenorphine after fentanyl, and the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are not in the withdrawal denominators (685 of the 742 who had ever taken it after fentanyl; editors' calculation) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). Recall at treatment entry may favour memorable bad experiences.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: fentanyl use (probably or definitely); the shortest time ever waited after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine or methadone, in categories within 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, 1 week, 1 month or 1 year, or never (Methods, PDF p. 2; Table 1, PDF p. 7). Urine fentanyl at admission only as reported by the respondent.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded: the buprenorphine dose and formulation (the table note lists sublingual, buccal, transdermal, injectable and implant brands), whether it was prescribed and supervised or obtained otherwise, and how many times it was taken after fentanyl.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or reported (other opioids, sedatives, stimulants or adulterants).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the time since fentanyl before buprenorphine is the exposure, recalled as the shortest wait ever.

comparison.controls: Within the survey: waiting-time categories compared with an unnamed reference category, which the editors' reproduction identifies as the people whose shortest wait was within 1 month (37 for buprenorphine, of whom 5 recalled severe withdrawal; 8 for methadone, of whom 2); methadone taken after fentanyl as a comparator medication; and the 152 who had taken both.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Amount, frequency and duration of fentanyl use, tolerance, whether withdrawal had already begun before buprenorphine was taken, buprenorphine dose and setting, and other drugs used.

outcomes.instruments: A single self-rated item on withdrawal symptoms when taking buprenorphine or methadone after fentanyl (none, mild, moderate, severe) and a single item on whether the medication decreased withdrawal (no, mild or moderate decrease, complete alleviation) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). No validated withdrawal scale; the question wording is not given in the paper (descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1, not among the files).
outcomes.validity_norms: None reported; retrospective recall of an unspecified occasion or occasions.
outcomes.operationalization: Precipitated withdrawal is taken to be self-rated severe withdrawal after taking buprenorphine following fentanyl. The survey does not separate withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine from withdrawal it failed to relieve; the authors themselves explain severe withdrawal after methadone as insufficient opioid effect (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 8 odds ratios (4 waiting-time categories by 2 medications) at p<0.05.

analysis.effect_sizes: Withdrawal after buprenorphine taken after fentanyl (N=685, the people whose shortest wait was within 1 month): severe 250 (36.5%), moderate 136 (19.9%), mild 122 (17.8%), none 177 (25.8%); after methadone (N=200): severe 30 (15.0%), moderate 29 (14.5%), mild 44 (22.0%), none 97 (48.5%) (Table 1, PDF p. 7). Odds ratios for severe withdrawal with buprenorphine: within 24 h 5.202 (95% CI 1.979–13.675), p=0.001; within 48 h 3.352 (1.237–9.089), p=0.017; within 72 h 2.222 (0.780–6.329), p=0.135; within 1 week 2.133 (0.687–6.620), p=0.190; with methadone (N=199): 0.616 (0.117–3.247), 0.300 (0.035–2.606), 0.316 (0.036–2.750), 0.250 (0.019–3.342) (Table 1, PDF pp. 7–8). Editors' calculation: every printed odds ratio, interval and p value is reproduced exactly by unadjusted 2×2 comparisons against the within-1-month group, using the Table 1 group sizes, the printed severe counts for under 24 h (152) and 24–48 h (55), and severe counts of 25, 13 and 5 at 48–72 h, 72 h–1 week and 1 week–1 month (methadone 23, 2, 2, 1 and 2), which also match the bars of Figure 1 (measured at 300 dpi) and add up to 250 and 30. On these counts, the share recalling severe withdrawal within each waiting group was, for buprenorphine, 44.8% under 24 h (152/339; Wilson 95% CI 39.6–50.2), 34.4% at 24–48 h (55/160), 25.8% at 48–72 h (25/97), 25.0% at 72 h–1 week (13/52) and 13.5% at 1 week–1 month (5/37); for methadone 17.0% (23/135), 9.1% (2/22), 9.5% (2/21), 7.7% (1/13) and 25.0% (2/8). Overall proportions (Wilson 95% CI, editors): 36.5% (33.0–40.2) after buprenorphine and 15.0% (10.7–20.6) after methadone.
analysis.covariates: None reported (the reproduction shows the odds ratios are unadjusted).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The questionnaire wording, survey period and descriptive statistics are in Appendix 1 (not among the files); the reference category of the regression is not named; the severe-withdrawal counts for the 72-h, 1-week and 1-month groups appear only as bars in Figure 1.
analysis.power: Not reported. The reference groups (37 and 8 people, by the editors' reproduction) make every odds ratio imprecise, the methadone ones extremely so.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 685 people entering treatment who said they had taken buprenorphine within a month after using fentanyl, 250 (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal when they took it, against 30 of 200 (15.0%) after methadone. Recall of severe withdrawal was more common the shorter the shortest reported wait: about 45% when it was under 24 h, 34% at 24–48 h, about 25% at 48 h to 1 week and 14% at 1 week to 1 month (editors' calculation from the printed counts and odds ratios).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and results say that, of those who waited less than 24 hours, 22.19% reported severe withdrawal; that figure is 152 of all 685, not of the 339 who waited less than 24 hours, of whom 44.8% did (editors' calculation) (PDF pp. 1, 3). The objective speaks of incidence (PDF p. 1) and the conclusion of greater risk relative to those who wait more than 48 hours (PDF p. 4), but the data are recalled at treatment entry, the shortest wait ever is not tied to the occasion of the withdrawal, nothing is adjusted, and the comparison group is the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month; people whose shortest wait was 48 h to 1 week still recalled severe withdrawal in about a quarter of cases (odds ratios about 2, not statistically significant), which the results call “no increase in odds” (PDF p. 3). Severe withdrawal after buprenorphine is labelled precipitated, although the survey cannot separate it from withdrawal that buprenorphine did not relieve, as the authors' own explanation of severe withdrawal after methadone shows (PDF p. 4). The discussion says buprenorphine preceded severe withdrawal in more than a third of the 1,163; the third is of 685 (PDF p. 3).

timeline.event: A qualitative study of buprenorphine experiences in the fentanyl era (Silverstein et al., 2019) and a commentary (Bisaga, 2019) are cited as the anecdotal evidence this survey supports (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, PDF p. 4).

A report of a method for starting people who use illicit fentanyl on buprenorphine/naloxone (Antoine et al., 2020, with Huhn) is cited among the case studies of precipitated withdrawal despite 2 to 3 days of observed abstinence (PDF p. 2).
The authors' study of protracted renal clearance of fentanyl in people with opioid use disorder (Huhn et al., 2020) is cited for the proposed mechanism (PDF p. 4).
Multisite emergency-department trial of buprenorphine starts reporting the incidence of precipitated withdrawal (title from the reference record; not read for this card)

replication.where_it_stands: The paper describes the earlier evidence as case reports and anecdotal accounts and cites no other survey. It cannot give the incidence of precipitated withdrawal at supervised starts; a later multisite trial in emergency departments is on the project's reference list (D'Onofrio et al., 2023) but was not read for this card.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse of the National Institutes of Health, grants T32DA007209 (NBV) and UG3DA048734 (ASH, KED) (Acknowledgments, PDF pp. 4–5).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (PDF p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and the University of Pennsylvania (Corporal Michael J. Crescenz VA Medical Center); Hobelmann and Huhn are also affiliated with Ashley Addiction Treatment, a treatment provider, and the data came from NLW Partners' Trac9 system, both named in the disclaimer. Two cited background studies are the authors' own (references 2 and 7), as is one of the low-dose induction papers (reference 13). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of buprenorphine starts in people who use fentanyl that records the time since last fentanyl use (with urine fentanyl and norfentanyl), withdrawal on a validated scale before and after the first doses, the dose, formulation and setting, and compares standard with low-dose starts, ideally by randomization.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Admissions to 49 US treatment facilities using one outcomes-tracking system suit the stated population of people entering treatment, but the facilities, states and period are not described, and people who use fentanyl outside these programmes are not in the frame.
Data came from routine admissions; whether every admission was asked, and how many answered, is not reported.

685 and 200 give the overall proportions reasonable precision (36.5%, Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2; 15.0%, 10.7–20.6; editors' calculation), but the odds ratios rest on reference groups of 37 and 8 people (editors' reproduction).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Only the age, sex, race and self-reported urine fentanyl of the 1,163 are given; facility type, setting, states, survey dates and questionnaire wording are not.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: No response or item-completion figures; the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are outside the withdrawal denominators without explanation; the methadone denominator is 200 in one part of Table 1 and 199 in another.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Precipitated withdrawal is identified by one self-rated item recalled for an unspecified occasion; no validated scale; withdrawal brought on by buprenorphine is not distinguished from withdrawal it did not relieve.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same questionnaire at admission for everyone, but reliability is not reported and answers refer to different occasions, doses and settings.

Key percentages are given with the wrong denominators in the abstract and results; the logistic regression is unadjusted with an unnamed reference group; no intervals for the proportions; the conclusion compares with people who waited more than 48 hours, who were not the reference group.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk of bias. The survey reports on a large group of people entering treatment, but its outcome is a single recalled rating that cannot separate precipitated from unrelieved withdrawal, its sample frame and response are not described, its timing comparison is unadjusted and tied to the shortest wait ever rather than to the occasion, and its headline percentages use the wrong denominators. It may be cited for this: among people entering treatment who said they used fentanyl and had taken buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl, about a third (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal, against 15% after methadone, and recall of severe withdrawal was more common the shorter the shortest wait (from about 45% under 24 h to about 14% at 1 week to 1 month; editors' calculation). It should not be cited for the incidence of precipitated withdrawal at supervised starts, for a safe waiting time, or for 22% as the rate among those who waited less than 24 hours.

key_findings.finding: Survey of 1,679 people entering treatment for opioid use disorder at 49 US addiction treatment facilities, collected by a third-party outcomes-tracking system (Trac9) at routine admission and analysed de-identified; the fentanyl questions went to those whose primary drug was opioids and who reported probably or definitely using fentanyl.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Methods (p. 1); Methods, Sample and Assessments (p. 2)

key_findings.finding: 1,163 (69.3%) reported probably (180; 10.7%) or definitely (983; 58.5%) using fentanyl before treatment; they had a mean age of 30.77 years (SD 10.23), were 70.6% male (821) and 80.4% White (935), and 43.9% (510) said their urine tested positive for fentanyl at admission.

Shortest wait after fentanyl before taking buprenorphine (N=1,163): within 24 h 339 (29.1%), within 48 h 160 (13.8%), within 72 h 97 (8.3%), within 1 week 52 (4.5%), within 1 month 37 (3.2%), within 1 year 57 (4.9%), never 421 (36.2%). For methadone: 135 (11.6%), 22 (1.9%), 21 (1.8%), 13 (1.1%), 8 (0.7%), 29 (2.5%), never 935 (80.4%).

Of the 685 who had taken buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl, 250 (36.5%) recalled severe withdrawal, 136 (19.9%) moderate, 122 (17.8%) mild and 177 (25.8%) none; of 200 who had taken methadone, 30 (15.0%) severe, 29 (14.5%) moderate, 44 (22.0%) mild and 97 (48.5%) none.
key_findings.locator: Results, Survey Results (p. 3); Table 1, second panel (p. 7)
key_findings.note: 685 equals the buprenorphine groups up to 1 month (339+160+97+52+37), so the 57 whose shortest wait was within a year are not included (editors' calculation). Wilson 95% CI 33.0–40.2% for buprenorphine and 10.7–20.6% for methadone (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: As printed, 22.19% (152 of 685) of the buprenorphine group and 11.56% (23 of 199) of the methadone group had waited less than 24 hours and recalled severe withdrawal; 8.03% (55 of 685) and 1.01% (2 of 199) had waited 24–48 hours and recalled severe withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results (p. 1); Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 3)
key_findings.note: The paper words these as rates among those who waited less than 24 (or 48) hours; they are shares of all 685 (or 199). Within each group (editors' calculation from the Table 1 group sizes): 152 of 339 (44.8%) and 55 of 160 (34.4%) for buprenorphine; 23 of 135 (17.0%) and 2 of 22 (9.1%) for methadone.

key_findings.locator: Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Table 1, fourth panel (pp. 7–8)
key_findings.note: The reference category is not named. Editors' calculation: all eight odds ratios, intervals and p values are reproduced exactly by unadjusted comparisons with the within-1-month group (37 people, 5 with severe withdrawal, for buprenorphine; 8 people, 2, for methadone).

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from Table 1, the printed odds ratios and Figure 1: severe withdrawal was recalled by 25 of 97 (25.8%) whose shortest wait was 48–72 h, 13 of 52 (25.0%) at 72 h to 1 week and 5 of 37 (13.5%) at 1 week to 1 month for buprenorphine, and by 2 of 21, 1 of 13 and 2 of 8 for methadone; with the printed counts for shorter waits these add up to the totals of 250 and 30.
key_findings.note: Not printed as numbers: reconstructed from the odds ratios and confirmed by the Figure 1 bars measured at 300 dpi (buprenorphine 3.63%, 1.87% and 0.72% of 685; methadone 1.0%, 0.49% and 1.0% of 199).

key_findings.finding: Among the 152 who had taken both medications after fentanyl, 69 (45.4%) recalled severe withdrawal after buprenorphine and 20 (13.2%) after methadone.
key_findings.locator: Results, Odds of Severe Opioid Withdrawal, 2nd paragraph (p. 3); Figure 1, right panel (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Complete relief of withdrawal was reported by 68 of 177 (38.4%) for buprenorphine and 43 of 97 (44.3%) for methadone; no decrease by 29 (16.4%) and 18 (18.6%).
key_findings.locator: Results, Survey Results (p. 3); Table 1, third panel (p. 7)
key_findings.note: The denominators (177 and 97) equal the numbers who reported no withdrawal symptoms after each medication; the paper does not say who was asked this question.

key_findings.finding: 483 of the 1,163 (41.5%) knew someone who used fentanyl and had precipitated withdrawal after taking buprenorphine.

In the introduction, the authors state that buprenorphine taken within 6 to 8 hours of a full agonist such as fentanyl can precipitate withdrawal by displacing it, and that case studies had reported precipitated withdrawal in people using fentanyl despite 2 to 3 days of observed abstinence.
key_findings.note: No source is cited for the 6–8 h statement; the case studies cited (references 2–4) include a 2003 article and a 2021 systematic review of micro-induction, by their titles (PDF p. 5).

key_findings.finding: The authors explain the finding by fentanyl accumulating in fat with repeated use and taking weeks to clear through the kidneys (citing their own study), and buprenorphine displacing it, which may add to precipitated withdrawal within 48 hours of fentanyl use even when clinicians follow conventional induction procedures; they suggest severe withdrawal after methadone reflects too little opioid effect early in treatment, since first outpatient doses are capped and methadone takes more than a week to reach steady levels.
Conclusion: people who take buprenorphine within 24 to 48 hours of fentanyl use are at significantly greater risk of severe withdrawal than those who wait more than 48 hours.
key_findings.note: Editors' reproduction: the model's reference group was the 37 people whose shortest wait was 1 week to 1 month, not everyone who waited more than 48 hours (see reporting issues).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and results give 22.19% (152/685) as the share reporting severe withdrawal among those who waited less than 24 hours, and 8.03% (55/685) among those who waited less than 48 hours; both use all 685 as the denominator. The same applies to methadone (11.56% = 23/199; 1.01% = 2/199).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract halves the rate for the group it names. Editors' calculation: within the groups named, the shares are 44.8% (152/339) and 34.4% (55/160) for buprenorphine and 17.0% (23/135) and 9.1% (2/22) for methadone.

reporting_issues.issue: The Survey Results paragraph prints 29.1% (n=339/685) and 11.6% (n=135/200), but 29.1% and 11.6% are shares of 1,163, and its 36.5% (250/685) reads as if it referred to the 339 who waited less than 24 hours, whereas it refers to all 685.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paragraph is easily misread; Table 1 gives the right denominators. Editors' calculation: 339/685 would be 49.5% and 135/200 67.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says buprenorphine preceded severe withdrawal in more than a third of the 1,163 people who reported fentanyl use; the third is of the 685 who took buprenorphine within a month after fentanyl.
reporting_issues.consequence: Editors' calculation: of all 1,163, the 250 are 21.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1 (left) plots each waiting group's severe cases as a share of all 685 (or 199), so its fall from about 22% to under 1% mostly reflects the smaller numbers of people with longer waits (339 down to 37, Table 1), not lower risk; the legend does not explain this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure should not be read as risk by waiting time. Editors' calculation: within-group shares fall from 44.8% to 13.5%.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference category of the logistic regression is not named, and the conclusion compares with people who wait more than 48 hours; the editors' exact reproduction of the odds ratios shows the reference was the 37 people whose shortest wait was within 1 month. People whose shortest wait was 48–72 h or 72 h to 1 week recalled severe withdrawal in about a quarter of cases (odds ratios 2.222 and 2.133, not significant), which the results describe as no increase in odds.
reporting_issues.consequence: The data show a gradient with time since fentanyl, not a safe point at 48 hours; the non-significant odds ratios reflect a reference group of 37.

reporting_issues.issue: The methadone denominator is 200 in the withdrawal-severity panel of Table 1 but 199 in the waiting-time panel and the odds model.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor. Editors' calculation: 30 severe cases are 15.0% of 200 or 15.1% of 199.

reporting_issues.issue: The denominators of the relief question (177 for buprenorphine, 97 for methadone) equal the numbers who reported no withdrawal symptoms after each medication; the paper does not say who was asked.
reporting_issues.consequence: If only people without withdrawal were asked, the comparison of complete relief (38.4% against 44.3%) concerns that subgroup only.

reporting_issues.issue: The objective is to estimate the incidence of buprenorphine-precipitated withdrawal, but the outcome is a single self-rated severity item recalled at treatment entry, not tied to the occasion of the shortest wait, without a validated scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures are recalled lifetime proportions, not incidence, and they include withdrawal that buprenorphine did not relieve as well as withdrawal it brought on.
